# `silk/num/f32`

<!-- Generated by silk doc-reference. Do not edit by hand. -->

IEEE binary32 values with deterministic representation, classification, and math operations.

## When to use
Use `f32` when binary32 storage, interchange, or bandwidth is part of the contract. Use `f64`
for general floating-point work and unconstrained literals. It preserves substantially more
precision and is Silk's default floating type.

## Details
Basic arithmetic rounds to nearest with ties to even and never enables implicit fast-math
assumptions. Division by zero and overflow produce IEEE infinities or NaNs rather than integer-
style traps. Ordinary ordered comparisons return false for NaN and treat both zeros as equal;
[`totalOrder`](#totalOrder) distinguishes every encoding when deterministic ordering is required. The
`Order` conformance of `f32` uses the same total order, so `List<f32>.sort` puts negative NaNs
first, then `-0.0` before `+0.0`, and positive NaNs last.

[`toBits`](#toBits) and [`fromBits`](#fromBits) expose the exact binary32 representation, including signed zero and
NaN payloads. The source-defined rounding, extrema, sign, and square-root helpers canonicalize
NaN results so native and WebAssembly execution agree on their bits.

The trigonometric, inverse trigonometric, exponential, logarithmic, power, cube root, [`hypot`](#hypot),
and [`fma`](#fma) functions never call a host math library. Each states its error bound in units in
the last place, returns the same bits on every target, WebAssembly included, and gives the
canonical quiet NaN for every NaN result.

## Gotchas
Converting to an integer discards the fractional part and traps for NaN, infinity, or a value
outside the destination range. The `checkedTo*` counterparts return `None` on exactly those
inputs instead of trapping. Converting a large integer to f32 can round it.

## Examples
### Inspect a binary32 boundary by its bits
```silk
import silk.num.f32

pub fn main() -> i32 {
  let rounded = f32.round(-0.25)
  if f32.toBits(rounded) != f32.toBits(-0.0) {
    return 1
  }
  if !f32.isNaN(f32.sqrt(-1.0)) {
    return 1
  }
  return 0
}
```

Import as `f32` with `import silk.num.f32`.

<a id="INFINITY"></a>

## `INFINITY`

```silk
pub const INFINITY: f32
```

Positive infinity with the binary32 bit pattern `0x7F800000`.

### Details

No source literal spells infinity, and a literal that rounds to infinity is rejected. Doubling
[`MAX`](#MAX) overflows to the infinity encoding.

<a id="NAN"></a>

## `NAN`

```silk
pub const NAN: f32
```

The canonical quiet NaN, with the binary32 bit pattern `0x7FC00000`.

### Details

No source literal spells NaN. Infinity minus infinity is NaN, and static evaluation always
produces the canonical quiet NaN for a NaN result.

### Gotchas

NaN compares unequal to every value, itself included. Test for it with [`isNaN`](#isNaN).

<a id="totalOrder"></a>

## `totalOrder`

```silk
pub fn totalOrder(left: f32, right: f32) -> bool
```

Reports whether `left` precedes or equals `right` in the IEEE total order.

### When to use

Use this function for deterministic ordering that includes NaNs and distinguishes signed zero.

### Details

Unlike ordinary comparison, this order distinguishes negative and positive zero and provides a
deterministic position for NaN encodings.

The order is: negative NaNs, negative infinity, the negative numbers, `-0.0`, `+0.0`, the
positive numbers, positive infinity, then positive NaNs. The `Order` conformance of `f32`, which
sorting and binary search use, follows it.

<a id="sqrt"></a>

## `sqrt`

```silk
pub fn sqrt(value: f32) -> f32
```

Computes the correctly rounded square root and preserves either signed zero.

### Details

IEEE requires square root to be correctly rounded, so its native and WebAssembly instructions
have one admissible numeric result.

### Gotchas

NaN and negative nonzero inputs return the canonical quiet NaN. Negative zero is not treated as
negative and returns unchanged.

<a id="tan"></a>

## `tan`

```silk
pub fn tan(value: f32) -> f32
```

Approximates tangent within one unit in the last place using deterministic result bits.

### Details

The tangent is computed in binary64 and rounded once to binary32, so the result stays accurate
for every finite input, including the largest. NaN and either infinity return the canonical
quiet NaN. Either signed zero returns unchanged.

<a id="atan"></a>

## `atan`

```silk
pub fn atan(value: f32) -> f32
```

Approximates arctangent within one unit in the last place using deterministic result bits.

### Details

The result is in `[-pi/2, pi/2]`. NaN returns the canonical quiet NaN, either signed zero
returns unchanged, and an infinity returns pi/2 with its sign.

<a id="atan2"></a>

## `atan2`

```silk
pub fn atan2(y: f32, x: f32) -> f32
```

Approximates the angle of the point `(x, y)` from the positive x axis within one unit in the
last place using deterministic result bits.

### When to use

Use this function instead of `atan(y / x)` to get the angle of a vector in every quadrant,
including when `x` is zero.

### Details

The result is in `[-pi, pi]` and takes the sign of `y`, including a signed zero `y`. A zero
`y` returns itself when `x` is positive or `+0.0`, and pi with the sign of `y` when `x` is
negative or `-0.0`. A zero `x` with nonzero `y` gives pi/2 with the sign of `y`. Two
infinities give an odd multiple of pi/4. A NaN in either operand returns the canonical quiet
NaN.


<a id="exp"></a>

## `exp`

```silk
pub fn exp(value: f32) -> f32
```

Approximates `e` raised to `value` within one unit in the last place using deterministic result
bits.

### Details

A result too large for `f32` is positive infinity, and one too small is positive zero.
Negative infinity returns positive zero, positive infinity returns itself, and NaN returns the
canonical quiet NaN. Either signed zero returns one.

<a id="log"></a>

## `log`

```silk
pub fn log(value: f32) -> f32
```

Approximates the natural logarithm within one unit in the last place using deterministic result
bits.

### Details

Either signed zero returns negative infinity, and one returns positive zero. Positive infinity
returns itself. NaN and any negative argument return the canonical quiet NaN.

<a id="pow"></a>

## `pow`

```silk
pub fn pow(base: f32, exponent: f32) -> f32
```

Approximates `base` raised to `exponent` within one unit in the last place using deterministic
result bits.

### Details

A negative `base` has a real power only for an integer `exponent`, and an odd integer gives a
negative result. A result too large for `f32` is an infinity, and one too small is a zero, each
with that sign.

### Gotchas

The special cases follow IEEE-754 `pow`:

- A zero `exponent` returns one for every `base`, NaN included, and a `base` of one returns one
  for every `exponent`, NaN included.
- A `base` of negative one with an infinite `exponent` returns one.
- A zero `base` with a negative `exponent` returns an infinity, negative only for `-0.0` with an
  odd integer `exponent`. With a positive `exponent` it returns a zero signed the same way.
- With an infinite `exponent`, a `base` whose magnitude is below one gives positive zero for
  positive infinity and positive infinity for negative infinity. A magnitude above one gives the
  reverse.
- A negative finite `base` with a finite non-integer `exponent`, and any other NaN operand,
  returns the canonical quiet NaN.

<a id="cbrt"></a>

## `cbrt`

```silk
pub fn cbrt(value: f32) -> f32
```

Approximates the real cube root within one unit in the last place using deterministic result
bits.

### Details

The result has the sign of `value`, so a negative argument has a negative root. Either signed
zero and either infinity return unchanged. NaN returns the canonical quiet NaN.

<a id="hypot"></a>

## `hypot`

```silk
pub fn hypot(x: f32, y: f32) -> f32
```

Approximates `sqrt(x * x + y * y)` within one unit in the last place using deterministic
result bits, without intermediate overflow or underflow.

### When to use

Use this function for the length of a vector or the distance between two points. It stays
accurate where squaring an operand would overflow to infinity or underflow to zero.

### Details

The result is never negative, and the signs of the operands do not matter. An infinite
operand returns positive infinity even when the other is NaN. Otherwise a NaN operand returns
the canonical quiet NaN.

<a id="fma"></a>

## `fma`

```silk
pub fn fma(left: f32, right: f32, addend: f32) -> f32
```

Computes `left * right + addend` with a single rounding, as the IEEE-754 fused multiply-add.

### When to use

Use this function for exact dot products, polynomial evaluation, and error terms, where
rounding the product separately loses the low half that the addend should cancel.

### Details

The result is correctly rounded on every target, so it has one admissible value. Targets with a
fused multiply-add instruction, AArch64 and x86-64 with the `fma` CPU feature, compute it with
that instruction. Other targets, WebAssembly included, compute it with binary64 arithmetic.

### Gotchas

A NaN operand, or an infinite product with a zero operand or an infinite addend of the other
sign, returns the canonical quiet NaN.

<a id="toU8"></a>

## `toU8`

```silk
pub fn toU8(value: f32) -> u8
```

Converts `value` toward zero to `u8`. Traps for NaN, infinity, or a result
outside the `u8` range.

<a id="checkedToU8"></a>

## `checkedToU8`

```silk
pub fn checkedToU8(value: f32) -> Option<u8>
```

Converts `value` toward zero to `u8`, or returns `None` when the truncated result is out of
range.

### When to use

Use this function when a NaN, an infinity, or an out-of-range magnitude is input data rather
than a program error. [`toU8`](#toU8) traps on exactly the inputs this function reports as `None`.

### Details

The fraction is discarded first, so the range test applies to the truncated value: a magnitude
below one is in range and yields zero. The truncated value is accepted when it is at least zero
and below `2^8`. Both bounds are powers of two and so are exact in binary32. A bound converted
from `u8.MAX` would round outward and wrongly admit an overflowing value.

### Gotchas

NaN and either infinity return `None`. A value in `(-1.0, -0.0]` truncates to negative zero and
converts to `0`, so its sign is discarded rather than rejected.

<a id="checkedToUsize"></a>

## `checkedToUsize`

```silk
pub fn checkedToUsize(value: f32) -> Option<usize>
```

Converts `value` toward zero to `usize`, or returns `None` when the truncated result is out of
range.

### When to use

Use this function when a NaN, an infinity, or an out-of-range magnitude is input data rather
than a program error. [`toUsize`](#toUsize) traps on exactly the inputs this function reports as `None`.

### Details

The fraction is discarded first, so the range test applies to the truncated value: a magnitude
below one is in range and yields zero. `usize` follows the selected target's pointer width, so
the bounds follow it too. The truncated value is accepted when it is at least zero and below
`2^32` on a 32-bit target or `2^64` on a 64-bit one.

Every bound is a power of two and so is exact in binary32. A bound converted from `usize.MAX`
would round outward and wrongly admit an overflowing value, and a bound fixed at 64-bit width
would admit values that trap on a 32-bit target.

### Gotchas

NaN and either infinity return `None`. A value in `(-1.0, -0.0]` truncates to negative zero and
converts to `0`, so its sign is discarded rather than rejected.

## `checkedToI32`

```silk
pub fn checkedToI32(value: f32) -> Option<i32>
```

Converts `value` toward zero to `i32`, or returns `None` when the truncated result is out of
range.

### When to use

Use this function when a NaN, an infinity, or an out-of-range magnitude is input data rather
than a program error. [`toI32`](#toI32) traps on exactly the inputs this function reports as `None`.

### Details

The fraction is discarded first, so the range test applies to the truncated value: a magnitude
below one is in range and yields zero. The truncated value is accepted when it is at least
`-2^31` and below `2^31`. Both bounds are powers of two and so are exact in binary32. A bound
converted from `i32.MAX` would round outward and wrongly admit an overflowing value.

### Gotchas

NaN and either infinity return `None`. A value in `(-1.0, -0.0]` truncates to negative zero and
converts to `0`, so its sign is discarded rather than rejected.

## `checkedToI64`

```silk
pub fn checkedToI64(value: f32) -> Option<i64>
```

Converts `value` toward zero to `i64`, or returns `None` when the truncated result is out of

### Details

### Gotchas

## `toIsize`

```silk
pub fn toIsize(value: f32) -> isize
```

Converts `value` toward zero to `isize`. Traps for NaN, infinity, or a result

<a id="checkedToIsize"></a>

## `checkedToIsize`

```silk
pub fn checkedToIsize(value: f32) -> Option<isize>
```

Converts `value` toward zero to `isize`, or returns `None` when the truncated result is out of
range.

### When to use

Use this function when a NaN, an infinity, or an out-of-range magnitude is input data rather
than a program error. [`toIsize`](#toIsize) traps on exactly the inputs this function reports as `None`.

### Details

The fraction is discarded first, so the range test applies to the truncated value: a magnitude
below one is in range and yields zero. `isize` follows the selected target's pointer width, so
the bounds follow it too. The truncated value is accepted when it is at least `-2^31` and below
`2^31` on a 32-bit target, or at least `-2^63` and below `2^63` on a 64-bit one.

Every bound is a power of two and so is exact in binary32. A bound converted from `isize.MAX`
would round outward and wrongly admit an overflowing value, and a bound fixed at 64-bit width
would admit values that trap on a 32-bit target.

### Gotchas

NaN and either infinity return `None`. A value in `(-1.0, -0.0]` truncates to negative zero and
converts to `0`, so its sign is discarded rather than rejected.
